doc.title: George Masso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997

title: Dance tempos, Jimmy Dorsey band and Tommy Dorsey
summary: Goodman's dance tempos; Masso with Jimmy Dorsey in 1948-49; Tommy Dorsey's breath control; Jimmy's musicianship; Dick Johnson's Artie Shaw band.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: Benny Goodman. Even the ballads that he did, you know he would never play a ballad too slowly. He would give it a nice dance tempo.
So even if people weren’t dancing, they could think about it.

That’s true. In those days it was wonderful because, you know I was with the Jimmy Dorsey band in 1949 — ‘48, which was the tail end of the big band era, but there were still a lot of people who were into big bands. And it was great because a lot of them would just hang around the bandstand, to sit and listen and watch. A captive audience.
Jimmy Dorsey was known for his breath control?

Marvelous breath control, you know, as a trombonist, he was one of my inspirations too, I should have mentioned him earlier, but he was such a great ballad player you know. And he had such control, I mean he could play right up in front of the microphone, very, very softly and let the microphone do a lot of work. But he had great control and beautiful sound.
Was he a good guy to work for?
Well I was with Jimmy. So Jimmy was a nice person to work for. Great musician too. I think unfortunately he lived in the shadow of Tommy, but he was a marvelous clarinet and saxophonist.
Gee some of the stuff he recorded back then was, from a technical standpoint, with all that double tonguing and all that, that was hard to reproduce.

Highly proficient technically. But he also had a lot in here. Sometimes he would play ballads, particularly on alto, and it would bring tears to your eyes. He was a good improviser too. I don’t think a lot of people realize this.
As a matter of fact, the Jimmy Dorsey Orchestra just played at Hamilton a couple of weeks ago.
I forget the fellow — the fellow who’s leading it now is a trombone player.

Yes. I met him recently, I can’t recall his name. But I do some things with the Artie Shaw band, led by Dick Johnson, who is a very close friend of mine, and we live in the same area. So I go out with him occasionally and do things. And once place we were playing they had two bands, the other band was the Jimmy Dorsey band.
